client: I've been really struggling since my grandfather passed away a few weeks ago, and with my final exams starting next week, I just can't seem to get my head together. Every time I sit down to study, I end up just staring at the wall or crying, and I've barely gotten through any of my material. I guess I'm here because people keep telling me therapy helps, but honestly I'm not sure anything can really fix what I'm feeling right now.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for sharing something so heavy — losing your grandfather while facing exams is an enormous amount to carry at once, and it makes complete sense that your mind is struggling to focus. The grief you're feeling isn't something that needs to be "fixed," and I want you to know that what you're experiencing — the crying, the wall-staring — is your mind and heart doing the very human work of mourning. I'm curious, when you say you're not sure anything can help right now, what does "help" look like to you — is it about the exams, the grief, or something else entirely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know... I think when I said "help," I meant I just want to stop feeling so heavy all the time, like there's this weight sitting on my chest that won't go away. I guess part of me hoped therapy would give me some kind of answer or trick to just get through the next few weeks, but hearing you say grief doesn't need to be fixed... I'm not sure if that makes me feel better or worse. It almost feels like you're saying I just have to sit with this, and honestly that scares me because I don't know if I can do that and still function.
therapist: That fear you're naming — "what if I can't sit with this *and* still function" — is so important, and I want you to know those two things aren't necessarily in conflict. Grief doesn't ask you to stop functioning; sometimes it just asks for a little space alongside everything else, and we can work together on finding ways to create that without your exams swallowing you whole. Can you tell me a little more about what "functioning" looks like for you right now — what would feel like even a small win this week?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, functioning right now just means getting through my study sessions without completely zoning out or ending up scrolling my phone for an hour because I can't focus. A small win would probably be finishing even one practice paper without breaking down halfway through, but that feels harder than it sounds when every quiet moment just fills up with thoughts about my dad. I guess I'm also a little skeptical that "making space for grief" is something I can actually schedule around exams — it sounds nice in theory, but I don't really know what that looks like in practice.
therapist: You mentioned your dad just now — and I want to gently check in on that, because earlier you spoke about your grandfather, and I wonder if there's more to that story that's been sitting with you. Your skepticism about "scheduling grief" is completely valid, and honestly, the goal isn't to box it in — it's more about small, intentional moments so it doesn't ambush you mid-practice paper. What would it feel like to try just one tiny experiment this week, like giving yourself five minutes before a study session to acknowledge what you're carrying, before asking your brain to shift gears?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying, and I don't think it's a bad idea in theory, but I honestly worry that giving myself five minutes to "acknowledge what I'm carrying" will just open a door I can't close again before I need to focus. Like, what if I sit with it for five minutes and then I'm just... wrecked for the next two hours instead of being able to study? My grandfather raised me for a big chunk of my childhood when my dad wasn't around, so there's a lot tangled up there, and I'm not sure I trust myself to keep it contained the way you're describing.
therapist: What you just shared about your grandfather raising you — that context makes everything feel so much weightier, and it makes complete sense that this grief isn't just grief, it's tangled up with your dad, your history, and so much more than an exam season. Your fear of "opening a door you can't close" is actually really wise self-awareness, not a weakness — and it tells me we should think about this differently, maybe less about opening that door and more about just leaving a small crack, something that feels *safe* and contained for you. What do you think would feel like a manageable amount — is there anything, even tiny, that has ever helped you feel just slightly less overwhelmed in a hard moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate you framing it that way, because "a small crack" feels a lot less terrifying than throwing the whole thing open. But honestly, even thinking about what helps... I'm drawing a blank, which is kind of embarrassing to admit. The only thing I can think of is that sometimes when it gets really bad, I'll go sit in the room where my grandfather used to watch TV, just to feel close to him somehow, but I don't know if that counts or if it even actually helps or if I'm just... torturing myself.
therapist: That absolutely counts — going to that room is a meaningful, instinctive way of staying connected to him, and there's nothing embarrassing about it at all. I notice as you described it, there was something quieter in how you said it, like maybe a part of you isn't fully sure you're allowed to find comfort there. Can I ask — when you're sitting in that room, what does it feel like in your body, even just for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It's... kind of hard to describe, actually. There's this heaviness in my chest when I first walk in, like the air itself is different in there, and then sometimes, just for a second, it's almost like I can breathe a little more. But then I feel guilty about that, like if I feel even slightly okay, it means I'm forgetting him or moving on, and I don't want to do that.
therapist: That moment of being able to breathe a little more — that's not forgetting him, that's actually your love for him still working, creating a space where you feel safe enough to exhale. The guilt makes so much sense, but I'd gently offer this thought: what if feeling okay for a moment isn't moving on *from* him, but moving *with* him, carrying him into the next breath? What do you think he would have wanted for you in that room?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I want to believe that, I really do. But it feels almost too convenient, like something people say to make the grief easier to swallow rather than something that's actually true. And if I'm being honest, I don't know what he would have wanted for me, because he's gone and I can't ask him, and that uncertainty just makes everything feel more hollow.
therapist: The way you said that — there's something that sounds almost very small and far away in your voice, like the words are coming from somewhere exhausted and tender, even quieter than what you're saying. I don't want to brush past that, because you're right — I can't promise you it's true, and the not-knowing, the not being able to ask him anymore, that's one of the most painful parts of losing someone. Can I just sit with you in that hollowness for a moment, rather than trying to fill it with something — what does it feel like to say out loud that you don't know what he would have wanted?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It feels... strange, actually saying it out loud like that. Like I've been carrying around this assumption that I knew him well enough to know, and now that I say it, I realize I was maybe just telling myself a story to feel less guilty about the choices I made after he died. And that's somehow worse than the not-knowing itself.
therapist: That took real courage to say, and what you just uncovered — that the story you were telling yourself was partly to manage guilt — that's a genuinely important and tender thing to notice about yourself. I want to ask gently: what are the choices you made after he died that you've been carrying guilt about, if you feel ready to share that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... after he died, I didn't go to the funeral. I told myself it was because I couldn't afford the flight, which was partly true, but honestly I was also just... scared of facing everyone, of breaking down in front of people I barely knew anymore. And I've been telling myself the money was the real reason for so long that I almost believed it, but sitting here right now, I think I knew even then that I was choosing not to go.
therapist: What you just admitted to yourself — not just to me, but to *yourself* — in this moment takes enormous honesty, and I want you to know that sitting with that truth is not a small thing. The fear of breaking down, of being vulnerable in front of people, is so deeply human, and it doesn't make you a bad grandchild; it makes you someone who was overwhelmed and doing the best they could in an impossible moment. I'm wondering — when you imagine the version of yourself who made that choice out of fear, what do you feel toward them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I feel... I don't know, it's strange. Part of me wants to feel compassion for that version of me, like you're suggesting, but mostly I just feel this heavy kind of shame when I picture myself walking out of that hospital room before she passed. Like, compassion feels like letting myself off the hook too easily, and I'm not sure I deserve that yet.
therapist: The way you said that — softly, carefully — feels like someone handling something very fragile, and I think that fragility *is* you being gentle with yourself, even if it doesn't feel that way yet. I also want to gently notice that you said "hospital room" just now — which makes me wonder if there's more to this story than the funeral, and if the grief you're carrying is even more layered than we've touched on so far. Can you tell me a little more about that moment you're picturing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
